extracted.intended_audience: ARIPO patent examiners and patent applicants (claim drafters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting, interpreting and examining patent claims under ARIPO Rules (particularly Rule 7), including claim form, categories, clarity, support and sufficiency requirements. Aimed at determining compliance and inviting amendments where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part form of claim (Rule 7(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim may be presented in a two-part form: the first part recites the known combination of features (prior art portion) and the second or "characterizing portion" states the technical features which, in combination with the first part, it is desired to protect (the invention's additions to the prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite applicant to use the two-part form where invention is a distinct improvement in an old combination; do not force two-part form where inappropriate (e.g., combination of known elements of equal status, modification of known chemical process, complex systems with interrelated parts, new chemical compounds not falling within a known class). Purpose: allow reader to see clearly which features are part of prior art. Use other forms if two-part gives a distorted/misleading picture. Place reference signs in parentheses after features, if drawings make features more intelligible; such signs are aids and not limiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims may contain chemical/mathematical formulae and tables (but not drawings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim, as well as the description, "may contain chemical or mathematical formulae" but not drawings. "Any claim may contain tables" but only when the subject matter of the claim makes the use of tables desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the word "desirable," examiners should not object to tables in claims where convenient. Use drawings only by reference signs; drawings themselves must not be included inside claim text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must not rely on references to description or drawings except when absolutely necessary (Rule 7(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must not, in respect of technical features, rely on references to the description or drawings (e.g., "as described in part ..." or "as illustrated in Figure 2"). Such reliance is only permitted where it is "absolutely necessary."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite applicant to show absolute necessity if they rely on description/drawings. Exceptions: peculiar shapes illustrated only in drawings that cannot be readily defined in words or by simple formula; chemical products definable only by graphs or diagrams. Prefer reference signs in claims rather than textual references to the description/drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference signs to drawings are aids and not limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: If drawings exist and relating claim features to drawing features renders claims more intelligible, place appropriate reference signs in parentheses after the features in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference signs should be used in both parts of two-part claims. They are not to be construed as limiting the claim scope but merely as aids to understanding the defined subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of claim — product (entity) and process (activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two basic kinds of claim: claims to a physical entity (product, apparatus, substance/composition) and claims to an activity (process, use). Claims worded differently may fall in the same category (e.g., "system" vs "apparatus").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given for product claims (steering mechanism, woven garment, insecticide, communications system) and process claims. It is permitted to include claims of different categories in the same ARIPO application provided compliance with Administrative Instruction 22(6). Examiner should avoid over-rigid objections to differently worded claims of similar effect. Presence of different kinds of claims may assist applicant in later national-stage protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention and proliferation of independent claims (Rule 7(6), 7(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of unity: whether a group of inventions is so linked as to form a single general inventive concept shall be made without regard to whether inventions are claimed separately or as alternatives in a single claim. Examiner should take exception to unnecessary proliferation of independent claims but not to two or more independent claims in same category if there is a unifying inventive concept and claims as a whole are concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider remarks about claims of apparently similar scope. Situations where separate independent claims may be appropriate: improvements in two separate but interrelated articles sold separately (plug/socket), single-phase vs poly-phase electrical arrangements, group of new chemical compounds with several manufacture processes. Invite amendments if proliferation creates obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and dependent claims (Rules 7(4)(b), 7(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: All applications will contain one or more independent main claims directed to essential features. Dependent claims concern specific forms and must include reference to the claim they depend on and be construed as including all limitations of that claim. Multiple dependent claims include all limitations of the particular claim in relation to which considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific forms construed broadly as more specific definitions or different embodiments. Subject to Administrative Instruction allowances, reasonable number of dependent claims is permitted even where dependent claim features could constitute separate inventions. Group dependent claims together practically to enable association; invite amendment if arrangement creates obscurity. Claims may contain alternatives if similar and fairly substitutable and do not make the claim obscure. A claim may refer to another claim of a different category (e.g., "Apparatus for carrying out the process of Claim 1...")—this is not a dependent claim as defined but is permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of claims — ordinary meaning to person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be interpreted the same way for search and examination. Each claim should be read giving words the ordinary meaning and scope attributed by a person skilled in the relevant art, unless the description gives a special meaning by explicit definition or otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply ordinary meaning for both search and examination purposes; consider description if special meaning is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Use" claims (Rule 7(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to a substance or composition for a particular use should generally be construed as meaning a substance/composition which is in fact suitable for the stated use. A known product that is the same but in a form unsuitable for the stated use does not deprive novelty; if in a form suitable for that use though never described for that use, it would deprive novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim phrased "... for use as a medicament" is regarded as restricted to the substance when presented/packaged for that use. Consider form/packaging and suitability for the use when assessing novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of the preamble on claim evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of the preamble on evaluation for search/examination should be determined case by case. Statements in the preamble reciting purpose or intended use must be evaluated to determine whether recited purpose results in a structural or process-step difference between the claimed invention and prior art. In two-part claims, the preamble is regarded as a limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim begins with "Apparatus for carrying out the process...", construe as apparatus suitable for the process. Apparatus that otherwise has all features but is unsuitable for stated purpose should not normally be within scope. Examples: "machine for cutting meat" construed as machine adapted to cut meat; "mold for molten steel" implies limitations like melting point, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open and closed claims — transition phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should consider which transition phrase is used (e.g., "consisting of", "comprising", "characterized by", "consisting essentially of") because the subject matter to be searched depends on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (a) "Closed" transition phrase: claim cannot include elements/steps beyond those set forth (e.g., "consisting of A, B and C"). Note that some Authorities may treat "consisting of" as equivalent to "consisting essentially of." (b) "Open" phrase: claim can be construed as including non-recited components (e.g., "comprising A, B and C" includes A,B,C and D). (c) "Consisting essentially of" occupies middle ground, limiting to specified materials/steps and those that do not materially affect basic and novel characteristics; absent clear indication, construed as open for search/examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a limitation defines a means or step in terms of function or characteristics without specifying structure/material/act, that limitation should be construed as defining any structure/material/act capable of performing the function or having the characteristics, unless further structure is specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If means are further specified, interpret to include those specifications. Example: "valve means for restricting flow" interpreted to include the further specified limitation if present; otherwise construed to any means capable of performing that function. Separately assess whether such claims are clear/concise and whether disclosure is sufficient for a skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim defines a product in terms of the process by which it is made, the claim as a whole is directed to a product. Such a claim lacks novelty if a prior art product, even if made by an undisclosed process, appears identical or indistinguishable from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If product can only be defined by the process or the manufacturing process imparts distinctive characteristics, the examiner should consider the process steps in search and assessing patentability (e.g., welding producing particular properties). Novelty only questioned if an identical two-layer panel made by welding is found in prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product and apparatus limitations appearing in process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Product and apparatus limitations that appear in process claims must be taken into account for search and examination purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore product/apparatus features when they appear within a process claim; include them in the subject of search and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistency between claims and description
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is any serious inconsistency between claims and description, amendments to remove this should be invited from the applicant (e.g., description implies a technical feature essential to performance but not in claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant convincingly shows description incorrect, invite amendment of description instead. Example: embodiments in description/drawings fall outside claims — invite amendment of claims or description to remove inconsistency. Overlook inconsistencies that do not cause doubt as to meaning. Object to general statements that imply vague expansion of protection (e.g., claiming the "spirit" of the invention) or statements implying protection for individual features/sub-combinations when claims are directed to a combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of claims (Rule 7(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be clear for individual claims and the claims as a whole. Clarity is essential for forming opinions on novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability; terms should, as far as possible, be clear for the person skilled in the art from the wording of the claim alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must set forth the scope of the invention with a reasonable degree of clarity analyzed in light of the disclosure, prior art and interpretation by a skilled person. Breadth is not necessarily lack of clarity. Independent claim should specify essential features needed to define the invention except insofar as implied by generic terms (e.g., a "bicycle" need not list wheels). Process claims must necessarily produce the product when carried out reasonably; otherwise internal inconsistency and lack of clarity. For modified well-known products, specify what is modified and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of relative terms and terms of degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims using vague or relative terms ("thin", "wide", "strong") should be objected to unless the term has a well recognized meaning in the art. Terms of degree require that a skilled person be apprised of meaning either by disclosure of a measuring standard or by prior art/state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite applicant to define or excise the term if they can do so without extending subject matter beyond the filing. An applicant cannot rely on an unclear term to distinguish over prior art. Claims defined by result to be achieved should generally be objected to as lacking clarity unless result is the only way to define the invention and achievable without undue experimentation (with tests/procedures specified). Defining product solely by parameters is acceptable if parameters can be clearly and reliably determined by description or objective procedures recognized in art; non-recognized parameters or inaccessible measurement apparatus may be objectionable. Pay attention when words like "about" or "approximately" are used; determine whether meaning is sufficiently clear in context. If such words prevent the invention from being unambiguously distinguished from prior art, raise objection to lack of novelty or inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of other terms (trademarks, "preferably", negative limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks characterize commercial origin rather than properties relevant to the invention; expressions like "preferably", "for example" have no limiting effect and should be carefully considered so as not to introduce ambiguity. Negative limitations (disclaimers) are not per se ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite removal of trademarks in claims unless unavoidable or generally recognized as precise. Treat features following "preferably" etc. as optional (non-limiting). Negative limitations are acceptable where clear; they render claim unclear if used to claim by excluding what was not invented rather than clearly reciting what was invented. Negative limitations are clear when each recited limitation is clear or when boundaries of protection are clear (examples provided). If alternative elements are positively recited in description they may be explicitly excluded in claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and number of claims (Rule 7(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement for conciseness refers to claims collectively and individually. Undue repetition or an undue multiplicity of trivial claims may fail this requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should object to unnecessary repetition and proliferation of trivial claims; invite amendment to produce concise claim set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support in description (Rule 7(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims "shall be fully supported by the description." There must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim and the scope of the claims must not be broader than justified by the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general rule, a claim is regarded as supported unless there are well-founded reasons to believe a skilled person could not, on basis of filed information, extend the teaching of the description to the whole claimed field by routine methods. Support must relate to claimed features; vague statements or assertions with no technical content provide no basis. Raise objection of lack of support only if well-founded reasons exist and, where possible, support reasons by a published document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and complete disclosure / sufficiency (Rule 7(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of each claim must be supported by the description and drawings "in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person skilled in the art." Disclosure is sufficient if it enables the skilled person, as of the international filing date, to carry out the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skilled person may use general knowledge to supplement application. Reasonable trial and error is permissible; undue experimentation is not. Factors in assessing undue experimentation include: (i) breadth of the claims; (ii) nature of the invention; (iii) general knowledge of a person skilled in the art; (iv) level of predictability in the art; (v) amount of direction provided in the application, including references to prior art; and (vi) amount of experimentation required to carry out the invention on the basis of the disclosure. Breadth of claims is relevant because a skilled person must be able to carry out the entire scope. Representative examples and explanation of how to apply them across the claim scope may suffice, even in unpredictable arts, provided undue experimentation is avoided.
